finding.claim: DELETE /projects/:id deletes any project for any authenticated user because the authorization result is discarded.

trace.note: project loaded by ID with no ownership filter
authorized() returns a boolean that is computed and dropped; it never throws

finding.guards_checked: No check in the DELETE handler. authorize() (api.js:4-10) throws correctly but is not used here. Authentication is assumed from upstream middleware, which is not in this file.

verdict.guard_found: none. authorized() (api.js:12-14) returns a boolean, and its result is discarded as a bare statement at api.js:18, so it never blocks. authorize() (api.js:4-10) would throw correctly but is not called on the DELETE path (api.js:16-21). The only other file in the directory is api.js, so there is no visible upstream ownership check; upstream authentication middleware is not in the provided code.
verdict.reason: The DELETE handler at api.js:16-19 loads the project by req.params.id with no ownership filter, discards the boolean from authorized() at api.js:18, and deletes at api.js:19, so any authenticated user (low-privilege included) can delete any project; the trace matches the code exactly.

finding.claim: authorize() and authorized() use different admin checks: truthy !user.isAdmin versus strict isAdmin === true. A truthy non-boolean isAdmin passes PUT but fails DELETE.
finding.source: req.user.isAdmin, populated from an unverified upstream source
finding.sink: Access decision in authorize() (api.js:5), used by PUT at api.js:25

trace.note: authorize() grants access when user.isAdmin is truthy

finding.guards_checked: Strict equality exists in authorized() only. How isAdmin is set upstream was not verified.

verdict.guard_found: authorize() at api.js:5 throws on failure and is used by PUT (api.js:25). authorized() at api.js:13 returns a bool, but its result is discarded by the DELETE route at api.js:18, so it guards nothing. No auth middleware appears in api.js.
verdict.reason: The claim that a truthy non-boolean isAdmin "fails DELETE" is wrong: api.js:18 calls authorized(req.user, project) as a bare statement and ignores its return value, so DELETE proceeds for any caller and the strict === true check at api.js:13 never blocks anything. The real defect is that DELETE (api.js:16-19) has no effective authorization at all, which the candidate misses; the truthy-isAdmin PUT path (api.js:5, 25) also depends on how req.user.isAdmin is set upstream, which is not in the code provided.

finding.claim: A nonexistent project ID causes a TypeError (500) instead of 404. Combined with 403 and 200 responses, this lets callers enumerate which project IDs exist.
finding.source: req.params.id for an ID that is not in the store
finding.sink: resource.ownerId dereference in authorize() (api.js:5) and authorized() (api.js:13) when resource is undefined

trace.note: store.projects.get returns undefined for a missing ID (DELETE route)
authorized(req.user, undefined) dereferences resource.ownerId and throws
same lookup in the PUT route

finding.guards_checked: No null check on the lookup result in either route.

verdict.guard_found: none. No null check on the lookup in either route (api.js:17, api.js:24). authorized() at api.js:13 and authorize() at api.js:5 dereference resource.ownerId without a guard, so an undefined resource throws a TypeError. The only other check is the 403 thrown at api.js:8 for an existing project owned by someone else, which is the 403-vs-500 distinction the oracle relies on.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the code: Map-style lookup returns undefined for a missing ID (api.js:24), and authorize(req.user, undefined) throws a TypeError at api.js:5 with no catch in this file, while an existing non-owned project yields a 403 at api.js:8, so the PUT route gives a 500-vs-403 existence oracle reachable by any authenticated caller. The 500 depends on Express's default error handler, and the auth middleware that sets req.user and req.store is not in the directory, so I could not confirm the attacker's exact role; the flaw itself is still reachable by a low-privilege user.

finding.claim: PUT /projects/:id/name assigns req.body.name with no type or length validation and echoes the stored object back.
finding.sink: project.name assignment at api.js:26, returned via res.json at api.js:27

trace.note: req.body.name assigned directly to the stored project
stored project serialized back to the caller

finding.guards_checked: None in this file. Impact depends on the store implementation, which is not visible here.

verdict.guard_found: authorize() at api.js:4-10, called as a bare statement at api.js:25. It throws a 403 on failure, so the throw aborts the handler before api.js:26 runs. The call is not a discarded return value. authorized() at api.js:12-14 is a different, non-throwing function and is not called on this route.
verdict.reason: The trace lines at api.js:26-27 match the claim, but the only attacker who reaches the assignment is the project owner or an admin (api.js:5), who can already set that name, so there is no escalation, and the missing type/length check on req.body.name (api.js:26) is only a hygiene issue since no sink in this file interprets the value and the store is not visible.
